title: Balanced and Unbalanced Forces, and Moments
summary: How balanced and unbalanced forces change motion, the skydiver story, and how to calculate moments and balance seesaws and levers — with worked examples and a Checkpoint-style quiz.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Describe what balanced and unbalanced forces do to the motion of an object: start, stop, speed up, slow down or change direction. (8Pf.03)
Identify turning forces and calculate them with moment = force × distance from the pivot. (8Pf.04)

blocks.text: 2. Forces and resultant force

A **force** is a push or a pull. Forces are measured in **newtons (N)** with a newton meter (force meter). In a diagram we draw a force as an **arrow**: the arrow points in the direction of the force, and a longer arrow means a bigger force.
Most objects have several forces acting on them at once. The **resultant force** is the single force that would have the same effect as all of them together:

items: Forces in the **same direction**: **add** them.
Forces in **opposite directions**: **subtract** the smaller from the larger. The resultant acts in the direction of the **larger** force.
If the resultant force is **zero**, the forces are **balanced**. If it is not zero, they are **unbalanced**.

blocks.text: 3. Balanced forces
When the forces on an object are **balanced** (resultant force = 0), its motion **does not change**:

items: An object that is **still stays still**. A book on a table: its weight (down) is balanced by the support force of the table (up).
An object that is **moving keeps moving at the same speed in the same direction**. It does **not** slow down and stop.

blocks.title: A very common mistake
blocks.text: "If the forces are balanced, the object must be still." **Wrong!** Balanced forces mean **no change** in motion. A car moving at a steady 20 m/s on a straight road has balanced forces. Forces are needed to **change** motion, not to keep something moving.
4. Unbalanced forces
When the forces are **unbalanced**, there is a resultant force and the motion **changes**. What happens depends on the direction of the resultant force:

rows: in the **same direction** as the motion
A car driver presses the accelerator: driving force > air resistance + friction.
A cyclist stops pedalling: friction and air resistance slow the bicycle.
the object **starts to move** in the direction of the resultant
A car turning a corner; a ball hit by a bat.

blocks.text: **The skydiver — balanced and unbalanced forces in one story.** Checkpoint loves this example. Learn the five stages:

rows: weight **>** air resistance (air resistance is small at low speed)
air resistance **increases** as speed increases, but weight is still bigger
still speeds up, but more slowly
air resistance **>** weight (the big parachute has a large area)
air resistance falls as she slows until it **=** weight again — balanced
new, much slower constant speed for a safe landing

blocks.title: الفكرة الأساسية للقوى
items: القوى المتزنة (المحصلة = صفر): الجسم الواقف يفضل واقف، والجسم المتحرك يفضل ماشي بنفس السرعة وفي نفس الاتجاه.
القوى غير المتزنة: الحركة بتتغير — الجسم يسرّع، أو يبطّأ، أو يغيّر اتجاهه، أو يبدأ يتحرك.
المحصلة: لو القوتين في نفس الاتجاه نجمع، ولو عكس بعض نطرح، والاتجاه بيكون مع القوة الأكبر.

blocks.text: 5. Turning forces: moments

A force can make an object **turn** around a fixed point called the **pivot**. Opening a door, using a spanner, riding a seesaw and lifting the lid of a tin with a spoon are all examples. The turning effect of a force is called its **moment**.

blocks.title: The formula
blocks.text: **moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot**. Unit: **newton metre (N m)** when the distance is in metres, or **N cm** when the distance is in centimetres.

"Perpendicular distance" means the distance from the pivot to the force, measured **at right angles** to the force. In most Stage 8 questions the force pushes straight across the lever, so you just use the distance from the pivot to where the force acts.

blocks.caption: A 40 N force at the end of a spanner, 0.25 m from the pivot. Moment = 40 × 0.25 = 10 N m.

blocks.text: **To get a bigger moment** you can use a **bigger force**, or apply the force **further from the pivot**. That is why:

items: a long spanner undoes a tight nut more easily than a short one;
a door handle is on the edge furthest from the hinges;
it is easier to open a tin lid with a long spoon handle than with a coin;
on a seesaw, a light child sitting far from the pivot can balance a heavier adult sitting near the pivot.

blocks.text: 6. Balancing: clockwise and anticlockwise moments

A force on the **left** of a pivot pushing down turns the beam **anticlockwise**. A force on the **right** of a pivot pushing down turns it **clockwise**. If the total clockwise moment equals the total anticlockwise moment, the beam is **balanced** (it does not turn). This is called the **principle of moments**.

blocks.title: Principle of moments
blocks.text: For a balanced object: **total clockwise moment = total anticlockwise moment**. If one side is bigger, the object turns that way.

blocks.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 480 250" width="480" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16"><polygon points="240,150 218,190 262,190" fill="#d9d9d9" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="40" y1="190" x2="440" y2="190" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1.5"/><rect x="25" y="142" width="430" height="8" fill="#fff4d6" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1.8"/><rect x="146" y="98" width="44" height="44" fill="#eaf1fb" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1.8"/><rect x="338" y="98" width="44" height="44" fill="#eaf1fb" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1.8"/><text x="266" y="180">pivot</text><rect x="145.2" y="73.2" width="45.6" height="20" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="168" y="88" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" font-weight="bold">500 N</text><rect x="337.2" y="73.2" width="45.6" height="20" fill="#ffffff"/><text x="360" y="88" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" font-weight="bold">300 N</text><line x1="168" y1="220" x2="240" y2="220" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1.4"/><line x1="240" y1="220" x2="360" y2="220" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1.4"/><line x1="168" y1="213" x2="168" y2="227" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1.4"/><line x1="240" y1="213" x2="240" y2="227" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1.4"/><line x1="360" y1="213" x2="360" y2="227" stroke="#0f1b33" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="204" y="244" text-anchor="middle">1.2 m</text><text x="300" y="244" text-anchor="middle">2.0 m</text></svg>
blocks.caption: A balanced seesaw. Anticlockwise moment = 500 × 1.2 = 600 N m. Clockwise moment = 300 × 2.0 = 600 N m.

items: Anticlockwise moment (left) = 500 N × 1.2 m = **600 N m**.
Clockwise moment (right) = 300 N × 2.0 m = **600 N m**.
The moments are equal, so the seesaw is **balanced** — even though the forces are different. The lighter person balances the heavier one by sitting **further** from the pivot.

blocks.title: العزم
items: العزم = القوة × المسافة العمودية من محور الارتكاز، ووحدته نيوتن متر (N m).
علشان تزوّد العزم: زوّد القوة أو بعّد عن المحور — علشان كده أكرة الباب بعيدة عن المفصّلات.
الاتزان: مجموع العزوم مع عقارب الساعة = مجموع العزوم عكس عقارب الساعة. والمسافة دايمًا تتقاس من المحور.

blocks.text: 7. Worked examples

**Worked example 1** — In a tug of war, team A pulls the rope to the left with 1200 N and team B pulls to the right with 1050 N. (a) Calculate the resultant force. [1] (b) Describe what happens to the rope. [1]

items: (a) Opposite directions, so subtract: 1200 − 1050 = **150 N to the left** (give the direction!).
(b) The forces are unbalanced, so the rope (and team B) **starts to move to the left**, towards team A, and speeds up.
**Common mistake:** adding the forces (2250 N). Forces in opposite directions are subtracted.

blocks.text: **Worked example 2** — A car moves at a constant speed. The driving force is 2000 N. (a) What is the total of air resistance and friction? [1] (b) The driver presses the accelerator and the driving force rises to 2600 N. What is the resultant force and what happens? [2]

items: (a) Constant speed → balanced forces, so air resistance + friction = **2000 N**.
(b) Resultant = 2600 − 2000 = **600 N forwards** (1), so the car **speeds up** (1).

blocks.text: **Worked example 3** — A spanner is used to turn a nut. A force of 40 N is applied 0.25 m from the centre of the nut. (a) Calculate the moment. [2] (b) The nut needs a moment of 15 N m to turn. What force is needed at the same distance? [2]

items: (a) moment = force × distance = 40 × 0.25 = **10 N m**.
(b) force = moment ÷ distance = 15 ÷ 0.25 = **60 N**.
**Tip:** rearranging works just like the speed triangle: force = moment ÷ distance; distance = moment ÷ force.

blocks.text: **Worked example 4** — A 250 N child sits 1.6 m from the pivot of a seesaw. Where must a 400 N adult sit on the other side to balance it? [2]

items: Anticlockwise moment = 250 × 1.6 = **400 N m** (1).
Clockwise moment must also be 400 N m: 400 × d = 400, so d = 400 ÷ 400 = **1.0 m** from the pivot (1).
**Check:** the heavier person sits **closer** to the pivot — sensible.

blocks.text: **Worked example 5** — A plank is pivoted at its centre. On the left, a 6 N weight is 20 cm from the pivot. On the right, a 4 N weight is 25 cm from the pivot. Will the plank balance? If not, which way will it turn? [3]

items: Anticlockwise moment = 6 × 20 = **120 N cm** (1).
Clockwise moment = 4 × 25 = **100 N cm** (1).
The anticlockwise moment is bigger, so the plank is **not balanced** and turns **anticlockwise** — the left side goes down (1).

blocks.text: **Worked example 6** — Explain why a book resting on a table does not move, using ideas about forces. [2]

items: The weight of the book acts **downwards** and the table pushes **upwards** with a support force (1).
These forces are **equal and opposite / balanced**, so the resultant force is zero and the book stays still (1).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Thinking balanced forces mean an object must be stationary. A moving object with balanced forces keeps moving at a **constant speed**.
Thinking a moving object needs a resultant force to keep moving. A resultant force is needed only to **change** speed or direction.
Forgetting the **direction** of the resultant force, or adding forces that act in opposite directions.
Saying the skydiver's **weight** decreases. Weight stays the same; it is the **air resistance** that changes.
Measuring distances from the end of a ruler instead of **from the pivot**.
Mixing cm and m in one calculation, or writing the wrong unit (moments are in **N m** or **N cm**, not N).
Deciding which side of a seesaw goes down by comparing the forces only — compare the **moments**.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: **Calculate the resultant force** from a force diagram and give its direction.
**Describe the motion** for balanced or unbalanced forces: stays still / constant speed / speeds up / slows down / changes direction.
**Explain** a sequence such as a skydiver, a car setting off and braking, or a rocket launch (3-mark answers: compare the forces at each stage).
**Calculate a moment** with units, or rearrange to find a force or a distance.
**Balance problems**: seesaws and metre rules — total clockwise moment = total anticlockwise moment; say which way it turns if not balanced.
**Explain an everyday design**: long spanners, door handles, wheelbarrows, scissors.
Write the formula, substitute with units, give the answer with its unit.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Forces and moments — practice
blocks.intro: Answer every part. Type short answers in the box; for longer answers write yours on paper first, then mark it with the mark scheme.

questions.q: In what unit is force measured?
c: kilogram (kg)
newton (N)
metre (m)
newton metre (N m)
questions.e: Force is measured in **newtons (N)**. Kilograms measure mass, metres measure distance, and newton metres (N m) measure a **moment** (turning effect).

questions.q: A motor boat has a forward force of 500 N from its engine and a backward force of 200 N from water resistance. Calculate the resultant force on the boat.
questions.e: The forces act in **opposite** directions, so subtract: 500 − 200 = **300 N** (forwards, in the direction of the larger force). The boat speeds up.

questions.q: A car moves along a straight, flat road at a **constant speed**. Which statement is correct?
c: The driving force is bigger than the friction and air resistance.
There are no forces acting on the car.
The forces on the car are balanced.
The weight of the car is bigger than the support force.
questions.e: Constant speed in a straight line means the forces are **balanced** (resultant force = 0): driving force = friction + air resistance, and weight = support force. A bigger driving force would make the car speed up. There are still forces acting — they just cancel.

questions.q: A cyclist on a flat road stops pedalling. The only horizontal forces on the bicycle are now friction and air resistance, acting backwards. What happens?
c: The bicycle slows down.
The bicycle speeds up.
The bicycle moves at a constant speed.
The bicycle stops immediately.
questions.e: The forces are **unbalanced** and the resultant force acts **backwards** (opposite to the motion), so the bicycle **slows down**. It does not stop instantly — it gradually loses speed until it stops.

questions.q:
Write the missing word.
A skydiver is falling at a constant speed. Her weight and the air resistance on her are ________.
questions.e: Constant speed means the resultant force is zero, so weight (down) and air resistance (up) are **balanced** — equal in size and opposite in direction.

questions.q:
A skydiver jumps from a plane. At first she speeds up, but after some time she falls at a constant speed.
Use ideas about forces to explain why. [3]
questions.ms: 1 mark: at first her weight is bigger than the air resistance / the forces are unbalanced with the resultant force downwards, so she speeds up. 1 mark: as her speed increases, the air resistance increases. 1 mark: eventually air resistance = weight / the forces are balanced, so the resultant force is zero and she falls at a constant speed. Do not accept 'gravity gets weaker' or 'weight decreases'.
questions.e: (1) Just after she jumps, she is moving slowly, so air resistance is small. Her **weight is bigger than the air resistance**, so the resultant force is downwards and she **speeds up**. (2) The faster she falls, the **bigger the air resistance** becomes. (3) Eventually the air resistance **equals** her weight. The forces are **balanced**, the resultant force is zero, and she falls at a **constant speed**. Her weight does not change at any time.

questions.q: A force of 20 N pushes on a lever at a perpendicular distance of 0.3 m from the pivot. Calculate the moment of the force.
questions.e: moment = force × distance from the pivot = 20 × 0.3 = **6 N m**. (1 mark for the working, 1 mark for the answer with the unit N m.)

questions.q: Ben cannot undo a tight nut with a spanner. Which change will give the **biggest** turning effect with the same force?
c: Hold the spanner closer to the nut.
Push along the spanner towards the nut.
Use a shorter spanner.
Use a longer spanner and push at its end.
questions.e: Moment = force × distance from the pivot. With the same force, the moment is biggest when the **distance is biggest**, so use a **longer spanner and push at its end**, at right angles to it. Pushing along the spanner towards the nut gives no turning effect at all (the distance from the pivot to the line of the force is zero).

questions.p:
Question 9
Two children sit on a seesaw. The seesaw is balanced. The diagram is not drawn to scale.

questions.q: (b) Calculate how far from the pivot the 300 N child sits. Show your working.
questions.e: The seesaw is balanced, so clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment. 300 × d = 600, so d = 600 ÷ 300 = **2 m** (2.0 m).

questions.q: (c) The 300 N child now moves 0.5 m closer to the pivot. What happens?
c: The seesaw stays balanced.
The right side, with the 300 N child, goes down.
The left side, with the 400 N child, goes down.
Both ends of the seesaw go up.
questions.e: Now the 300 N child's clockwise moment is 300 × 1.5 = 450 N m, but the anticlockwise moment is still 600 N m. The anticlockwise moment is bigger, so the seesaw turns anticlockwise: the **left side, with the 400 N child, goes down**.

questions.q: Calculate the size of force F. Show your working.
questions.e: Measure every distance **from the pivot** (50 cm), not from the end of the rule. Anticlockwise: 3 N at 50 − 20 = 30 cm gives 3 × 30 = 90 N cm; 2 N at 50 − 40 = 10 cm gives 2 × 10 = 20 N cm. Total anticlockwise = 90 + 20 = **110 N cm** (1). Clockwise: F at 90 − 50 = 40 cm gives F × 40 (1). Balanced: F × 40 = 110, so F = 110 ÷ 40 = **2.75 N** (1). Common mistake: using the scale readings (20, 40, 90) as the distances.

questions.q: Explain why the handle of a door is fixed on the edge **furthest** from the hinges. [2]
questions.ms: 1 mark: the hinge is the pivot, so the handle is a large distance from the pivot. 1 mark: moment = force × distance, so a larger distance gives a larger moment / turning effect for the same force, so less force is needed to open the door. Do not accept 'it is easier' with no reference to distance or moment.
questions.e: The hinges are the **pivot**. Moment = force × distance from the pivot. With the handle at the far edge, the distance is as large as possible, so a **small force gives a large enough moment** to turn the door. A handle near the hinges would need a much bigger force.

questions.q: What is the name of the fixed point that a lever or seesaw turns around?
questions.e: The **pivot** (also called the fulcrum). Moments are always calculated using the distance from the pivot.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Resultant force: add forces in the same direction, subtract forces in opposite directions.
Balanced forces (resultant = 0): no change in motion — still objects stay still, moving objects keep a constant speed and direction.
Unbalanced forces: the object speeds up, slows down, starts moving or changes direction.
moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot (N m or N cm).
Balanced when total clockwise moment = total anticlockwise moment.
